title: It didn’t make sense.
paragraphs: It didn’t make sense.
That’s where it started.

Not with rain.
Not with thunder.
Not with a single drop falling from the sky.
Just a man… cutting wood in a dry place, under a clear sky, building something no one had ever seen.
And everyone around him thought he had lost his mind.
You would have too.

Because what do you call a man building a massive ship…
when there has never been a flood?

What do you call obedience…
when it contradicts everything your eyes can prove?
That’s the tension most people skip over.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

Noah didn’t just build an ark.
He built it in a world that had never experienced rain the way we know it.
“And God said unto Noah… Make thee an ark of gopher wood…” — Genesis 6:14

No explanation.
No weather forecast.
No visible evidence.
Just a command.
And silence.

Day after day, he hammered wood into shape while people walked by laughing.
Whispering.
Pointing.
You can almost hear it:

“You’re building what?”
“For what?”
“Rain? What rain?”
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because you’ve been there.

God told you to walk away from something…
and it didn’t make sense.

God told you to forgive…
and everything in you said they don’t deserve it.

God told you to let go…
but you couldn’t see what would catch you if you did.
And you hesitated.
Noah didn’t.
“Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.” — Genesis 6:22
Read that again.
He obeyed… before seeing anything.

No signs.
No confirmation.
No backup plan.
Just God’s word.
And here’s the part that hits deeper than most are willing to admit—
Delayed obedience is still disobedience.

You call it “waiting for clarity.”
God calls it hesitation.

You call it “being practical.”
God calls it unbelief.
Because obedience was never meant to feel logical.
It was meant to reveal who you trust.
Every swing of Noah’s hammer was a declaration:
“I believe God more than I believe what I see.”

And every day he kept building…
the gap between him and everyone else widened.
Because obedience separates.
It always has.
“For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.” — 1 Corinthians 1:18
Foolish… until it saves you.

That ark looked ridiculous…
until the sky broke open.

That obedience looked insane…
until it became the only place of safety.
And then suddenly—

The same people who mocked him…
needed what he had built.
But the door closed.
“And the Lord shut him in.” — Genesis 7:16
God saw it.

He saw every moment Noah kept going when it made no sense.
Every doubt he pushed through.
Every voice he ignored.
You knew.
You’ve heard God before.

Not always loud.
Not always dramatic.
But clear enough that you can’t honestly say, “I didn’t know.”
The real question isn’t whether God has spoken.

It’s whether you’re willing to obey…
when it costs you your comfort, your reputation, your logic.
Because there are only two outcomes.

You either look foolish now…
or you’re unprepared later.
There is no middle ground.
This is bigger than Noah.

Because the same God who warned about a flood…
has already warned about judgment.
“As it was in the days of Noah, so shall it be also in the days of the Son of man.” — Luke 17:26

People eating.
Drinking.
Living like nothing is coming.
Until it does.
And the only refuge is not an ark made of wood—
It’s Jesus Christ.
The ark was a shadow.
Christ is the reality.
“I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved.” — John 10:9
There it is.

Not works.
Not effort.
Not trying harder.
Salvation is not you building something for God.
It’s you entering what Christ already finished.
Noah built the ark.
Jesus became it.
And now the door is still open.
But not forever.
So here you are.

Standing in a dry place…
hearing something that doesn’t fully make sense…
feeling the weight of a decision you’ve been avoiding.
And you already know.
If something in you is stirring, say it.
“I will obey.”

Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s easier.
Now.
Because someone you know is still laughing at the idea of surrender—

Not to argue.
But because they need to hear this before the door closes.
